newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian opposition to boycott parliament opening.
newsitem.headline: Albanian opposition to boycott parliament opening.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, defeated in elections last month, said on Monday it would boycott the first session of parliament to protest at the conduct of the polls.
Berisha has not yet convened the new parliament, and his Socialist opponents warned on Sunday that if he failed to issue the decree, they would call the first session themselves.

"The elections of June 29 were held in a climate of violence and terror exercised by Socialist gangs against supporters of the Democratic Party and the population in general," said a statement issued after a meeting of the party's National Council on Sunday.

It complained that the Democrats had been unable to campaign in the south for the elections, which were described by monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe as acceptable, if far from perfect.
Diplomats say the Democrats' losses even in Tirana and former strongholds such as Kavaje put paid to any serious claims of manipulation.
Berisha's Socialist party opponents and their coalition allies won a total of 117 seats to the Democrats' 27.
Berisha says he has no wish to cohabit with a Socialist government and will resign once he has "fulfilled his constitutional obligations", but he shows no immediate sign of stepping down.
He met leaders of his Democrats and smaller parties on Saturday to discuss when parliament should meet and who should be prime minister, but Socialist leaders refused to meet him.
The president has indicated that he would prefer the interim prime minister, Bashkim Fino, to stay on as premier rather than Socialist leader Fatos Nano, the party's preferred candidate.
The Democratic Party's 105-member National Council said the party should be reformed to become a "powerful, constructive and loyal opposition".
There have been calls for the party to distance itself from Berisha, but it said he should be given a mandate to lead the party until a full congress planned for October.
Much of the country is still ruled by armed gangs and most Albanians are eager to see a new government take charge and start restoring law and order.

Diplomats pressing for parliament to convene say they are concerned that there may be no prime minister to attend a donors' meeting in Rome at the end of July to discuss aid for the shattered country.
